scenes.title: Cold open: the plan vs the new plan
scenes.vo: NASA's next Moon mission was supposed to land here. Now it won't even leave Earth orbit.
shots: hard cut, zoom out from Moon to Earth, LEO ring lights up
scenes.sfx: 0.0 low sub hit; 1.3 whoosh-reverse into cut; 1.4 impact + silence 0.2 s

scenes.title: The surprising fact
scenes.vo: In April, four astronauts flew around the Moon on Artemis Two. And the next crew's rocket won't even carry the stage that sends Orion toward the Moon. In its place: a metal barrel with no engine.
shots: upper stage slides out, spacer slides in
scenes.sfx: tick on each on-screen word; metallic clank on 'barrel'

scenes.title: Why it matters + promise
scenes.vo: NASA made this change back in February, and in October it published the full plan: fourteen days in orbit, two Moon landers, and one test that has to work before anyone lands near the lunar South Pole. Here's what they'll actually do up there, and why NASA decided the Moon can wait a year.
shots: pan across, highlight two docking points
slow push to South Pole direction
scenes.sfx: music bed enters at 'Here's what' (low, pulsing)

scenes.title: What NASA changed in February
scenes.vo: Artemis Two's flight took ten days: launch on April first, a seven-hour lunar flyby on April sixth, splashdown off California on April tenth. But by then the plan for the next mission had already changed. On February twenty-seventh, NASA rewrote the order of the Artemis program. Artemis Three had been the landing. It became a test flight in low Earth orbit, set for twenty twenty-seven, and the first landing moved to Artemis Four, targeted for twenty twenty-eight. NASA also promised at least one landing every year after that. At the announcement, NASA's leadership argued that rare flights are a problem in themselves: crews and launch teams lose practice between missions, and changing the rocket and spacecraft after every flight adds risk instead of removing it.
shots: Artemis III block slides from 'LANDING' to 'EARTH ORBIT'
scenes.sfx: soft paper/whoosh on each timeline move

scenes.title: The hardware already exists
scenes.vo: And this isn't a paper mission. The four main engines for Artemis Three reached Kennedy Space Center in July. The Orion capsule and its service module were joined in late July. On September thirtieth, technicians put the nose cones on the twin boosters, finishing the stack. More than two hundred and fifty parts from Artemis Two's Orion are being reused on later missions, and NASA says reused parts move some installation work up by about three months. Even the launch tower is being turned around for its next flight nearly fifty percent faster. And that missing upper stage? It isn't scrapped. NASA reassigned it to Artemis Four, the mission that actually has to reach the Moon.
shots: slow vertical pan (portrait in 16:9 with blurred fill)
upper stage moves from A-III stack to A-IV stack
scenes.sfx: room tone of a high bay (library SFX), light mechanical clicks

scenes.title: Who flies
scenes.vo: The crew is Randy Bresnik, Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio of NASA, and Luca Parmitano of the European Space Agency. In September they trained with Navy helicopter crews off San Diego, practicing being hoisted out of the water after splashdown. They've drilled escaping a capsule underwater, trained in their orange survival suits, and tasted nearly two hundred items of space food. Their mission will be about two weeks long, and it will never get farther than a few hundred miles from home.
shots: names type on over Earth limb graphic, no portraits
4 training items tick in, icons only, no crew photos
Moon distance bar vs LEO ring

scenes.title: Three launches
scenes.vo: Artemis Three needs three launches. First, Blue Origin launches a test version of its Blue Moon lander. It can wait in orbit for up to thirty days. Then the crew launches on NASA's SLS rocket from Florida. Starship goes up after the crew is already in orbit.
shots: launch 1 arc, Blue Moon icon parks in orbit, 30-day counter
scenes.sfx: three distinct launch rumbles, each shorter

scenes.title: The orbits
scenes.vo: The orbits are precise. The Blue Moon test article circles about two hundred seventy-three miles up. Orion starts in a long, stretched orbit, from eighteen to more than eleven hundred miles, then rounds it out near three hundred forty-five. Starship flies lower still. Every number here comes from NASA's flight profile.

scenes.title: Dock one: Blue Moon
scenes.vo: First docking: Orion pulls up alongside the Blue Moon lander. While they're joined, Orion's own software flies both spacecraft. Then the hatch opens. Up to two astronauts, in their orange survival suits, float into a lunar lander for the first time since Apollo. They spend about two days checking its cabin, controls and life support. Riding along is a dummy the weight of a spacesuit, wired with sensors, reporting what the cabin really feels like.
shots: Orion approaches, side-by-side dock, 'ORION SOFTWARE IN CONTROL'
hatch icon opens, 2 figures move across

scenes.title: Dock two: Starship
scenes.vo: Second docking: Starship. The test vehicle is a hundred seventy-one feet tall, about fifty-two meters, with a docking port in its nose. Orion meets it nose to nose, and this time SpaceX flies the pair. It lasts up to two hours, and nobody goes inside. NASA and SpaceX are still deciding exactly which control and communication tests to run.
shots: Starship icon at true scale next to Orion (171 ft)
crew icon stays in Orion, red X on Starship hatch

scenes.title: Home
scenes.vo: After about fourteen days, Orion comes home and splashes down in the Pacific, off the coast of California, the same ocean where Artemis Two landed in April.

scenes.title: Why docking first
scenes.vo: So why test this in Earth orbit? Because on Artemis Four, the landing depends on exactly this step. Orion can't land. A commercial lander has to meet it, take astronauts down near the South Pole, and bring them back. If that handoff fails near the Moon, the crew is days from home. In low Earth orbit, they're hours away.
shots: Artemis IV path draws out to Moon, handoff point flashes
ARTEMIS IV: HANDOFF AT THE MOON
scenes.sfx: tension drone builds; cut to silence on 'hours away'

scenes.title: Apollo did this too
scenes.vo: If this sounds familiar, it should. In March nineteen sixty-nine, Apollo Nine tested the lunar module in Earth orbit. Four months later, Apollo Eleven landed.

scenes.title: What is still unknown
scenes.vo: What we don't know yet: a launch date. NASA says twenty twenty-seven; its administrator told reporters in October that next summer is still the target. The rocket's fueling test at the pad is still ahead. And NASA hasn't said which lander will carry the first crew down on Artemis Four.
shots: open items flash: tanking test, lander choice

scenes.title: Close
scenes.vo: So the next Moon mission stays close to home, on purpose. If both dockings work, the following crew goes all the way down. Artemis Four is the landing. Artemis Three is the test it can't skip.
scenes.sfx: music resolves; 1 s tail; end screen 10 s (silent, not counted)
